label: fiction
title: The Borrowed Coat
setting: The Halden Cooperative Gallery occupies a converted warehouse in the fictional city of Velmara. Co-founders Nera Vale and Iona Venn built it over twelve years, but a dispute over finances and control had divided them by the night Nera died. Reception faces the lobby; a staff corridor and alarmed rear door are out of sight from the desk. Three staff members remained during the final exhibition setup.
elements: The accused caused the victim’s death.
The accused intended to kill or cause really serious injury.
The killing was not legally justified or excused.
hook: After a bitter argument, Iona Venn asks assistant Elia Marr to walk out wearing Iona’s red coat. Elia does it. Seven minutes later, Nera Vale calls reception from upstairs—and is dead soon after. The jury must decide whether Iona stayed to kill her, or left by the rear stairs before that call.

accused.human: Iona Venn, 47, co-founded the gallery with Nera Vale and managed its building and apprentices. Their professional partnership had become bitter, though both still planned to finish the community exhibition. Iona’s sister and former apprentices sit behind the defence table. That history explains relationships and possible motive; it does not prove identity.
accused.if_guilty: Any sentence is a matter for the judge after the verdict and must play no part in the jury’s decision.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: Nera Vale was deliberately killed after her 9:12 call. The prosecution must prove Iona Venn caused that death and intended death or really serious injury. Its case is circumstantial: Iona arranged for Elia to leave in her coat while Iona’s dispute with Nera reached its end upstairs. Elia requires caution, so test her against the transit card in the coat, the rear-door times, the bracelet clasp, and Iona’s first interview. The prosecution says those independent strands prove Iona stayed and created a false departure.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: The defence accepts Nera was murdered and that Iona foolishly asked Elia to wear the coat. But the evidence must prove the killer’s identity, not merely expose a lie. Elia lied twice, received immunity, and never saw Iona after 8:45. The rear door opened before nine. A neighbour saw Iona in the alley around that time. The bracelet broke within a day, not necessarily near the death. Ask whether the prosecution could ever reasonably exclude Iona leaving before Nera’s final call.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: Elia’s immunity requires caution, but it doesn’t erase Iona’s own request: wear the distinctive coat, leave by the front, and take it home. The transit card independently confirms Elia carried out that deception while Nera was still alive upstairs. Nera was killed afterwards while holding part of Iona’s recently broken bracelet. Iona’s recorded first account omitted both the rear door and the folder struggle. The prosecution says motive, a staged departure, physical contact, and concealment leave no reasonable innocent explanation.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: Separate suspicion from proof. The transit card proves Elia travelled in the coat; it does not locate Iona. The rear door opened at a time consistent with Iona leaving, and a neighbour’s recollection supports that route. The clasp matches Iona’s bracelet, but the expert cannot distinguish the witnessed afternoon folder dispute from the time of death. Iona’s omissions can damage credibility without supplying the missing identity evidence. If the reasonable possibility remains that Iona left before Nera’s 9:12 call, the verdict must be Not Guilty.

epilogue: Nera Vale’s family asked the gallery to finish the community exhibition she had planned, but without turning her work into a memorial attraction. It reopened for one season under shared financial control. Elia Marr left the arts sector and declined every interview request. Former apprentices completed Nera’s unfinished display from her notes and kept one wall empty for new artists. Iona’s sister continued attending every hearing, while the cooperative’s members lived with questions the trial record could not answer.

beats.speaker: w1
beats.text: Tell us who Nera Vale was at the gallery. Nera chose young artists, remembered every installer’s birthday, and had spent months building that night’s free community exhibition. She and Iona founded the cooperative together, but staff knew they were arguing about its finances. When did you last hear from Nera? At 9:12, her name appeared on the internal line. She sounded alert, used my name, and asked me to bring the blue budget folder upstairs after I locked reception.

beats.speaker: w3
beats.text: What supported your medical opinion? I examined Nera the next morning, reviewed the paramedics’ observations and temperature readings, and considered the authenticated 9:12 call. Those sources support an estimate, not an exact minute. What could you conclude? Nera died between about 9:13 and 9:28. A single forceful blow to the back of her head with a hard blunt object fractured her skull and caused fatal brain injury. The angle and force weren’t consistent with a fall, natural illness, or self-infliction. They establish deliberate homicide and an intention at least to cause really serious injury, not the attacker’s identity.

beats.speaker: w3

You cannot use the injuries to decide whether the attacker arrived after the 9:05 lobby departure? Correct. Nor can your examination show whether Iona left through the rear door at 8:52? beats.text: Describe your role and what happened with the coat. I was a paid gallery assistant working under both founders. beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: The parties agree that Elia’s transit card began a journey near the gallery at 9:08 and continued away from the district. The same card was later recovered from the red coat’s inner pocket. Elia admits carrying that card and wearing the coat, so you may accept that she travelled away in it. The record supports that part of her account. It does not locate Iona.
beats.reveal_note: The transit card independently confirmed Elia’s journey and part of her account, but supplied no evidence about Iona’s location.

beats.speaker: acc
beats.text: Describe the disputes you had with Nera. At four, we both grabbed the blue budget folder. My bracelet caught; later I saw the clasp was gone. Around 8:40 we argued about gallery control. I walked down the staff corridor and used the rear door before nine because I couldn’t face another round. Why ask Elia to take the coat through the lobby? I wanted Nera to think I’d made a visible exit and stop looking for me. It was childish and deceptive, not a plan to hurt her.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: By agreement, the rear-door log shows the shared staff code used at 8:50, the door opening at 8:52 for eleven seconds, then relocking. Seven staff members knew that code; the log names no individual. Neighbour Tavi Lorin, who was walking a dog, told investigators she saw Iona step into the alley around that time and hurry toward the side street without looking back. Tavi had known Iona for years from gallery openings. The log and neighbour together support a rear exit near 8:52; neither proves Iona stayed away until after Nera’s death.
beats.reveal_note: The rear-door timing and neighbour recognition independently supported Iona’s exit account without proving she remained gone.

True, but I should have explained the rear route and coat request. You knew police were investigating Nera’s death? Yes. I was frightened, but knew the omissions made me look less involved.

beats.speaker: w3
beats.text: How was the clasp recovered and tested? I photographed it where I found it in Nera’s closed hand, placed it in a numbered sterile packet, sealed it, and recorded every transfer to the accredited materials laboratory. The seals and item number were intact when it returned. What did the agreed laboratory report find? Its shape, wear pattern, and fracture surfaces exactly fitted Iona’s bracelet. Microscopic oxidation showed the break was recent, meaning within roughly twenty-four hours before recovery. The method cannot narrow that broad window to an hour or identify how Nera came to hold it.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: Members of the jury, the prosecution must prove Iona caused Nera’s death, intended death or really serious injury, and acted without legal excuse. Homicide and intent are established; identity is disputed. Elia lied twice and received immunity, so examine her evidence carefully without automatically accepting or rejecting it. Circumstantial evidence may combine, but each strand keeps its limits. Iona’s lies may affect credibility; they do not prove murder or reverse the burden. She need not identify the rear-door user or explain the clasp. If, after considering all the evidence, you are not sure the prosecution proved every element beyond reasonable doubt, your verdict must be Not Guilty.
beats.reveal_note: The direction keeps the burden on the prosecution and identifies the unresolved location and timing issues without deciding them for the jury.

twist: The authors’ reference resolution is Not Guilty. Elia’s admission resolves who wore the coat; the contested question is whether Iona remained upstairs. The rear-door timing and neighbour recognition leave a reasonable possibility that Iona left before Nera’s 9:12 call. The strongest prosecution interpretation combines the staged departure, omitted interview details, and bracelet clasp. Those facts support suspicion, but do not prove identity beyond reasonable doubt.

jurors.label: Juror 2 — Anya
jurors.persona: Anya listens for what a witness personally observed and resists filling gaps with confidence.

agree: Can we separate what Elia saw from what she assumed?
The rear-door record doesn’t prove Iona left, but it means she may have.
pushback: I disagree. The transit record confirms Elia’s journey, not Iona’s location.
Elia lied twice; why would her unconfirmed assumption make us sure?
concede: I accept the coat request is real prosecution evidence. I still need the missing location link.
holdout: I’m not crossing that gap just because Iona’s explanation is awkward.
final: For me, the prosecution proved concealment, not who killed Nera.

jurors.label: Juror 3 — Bram
jurors.persona: Bram keeps replaying the vivid coat footage and needs prompting to name what it does not show.

agree: Right, the camera misses both the face and the rear door.
If Elia’s in the coat, why did I keep seeing Iona when I watched it?
pushback: But Iona arranged the trick. Doesn’t that count for something?
I can’t just shrug off Nera holding Iona’s clasp.
concede: Wait—I was treating the coat like a face. The recording never gave us one.
final: The picture looked complete before we asked what was outside its frame.

jurors.label: Juror 4 — Cora
jurors.persona: Cora writes down every time, then checks which person each timestamp actually locates.

agree: At 8:52 the rear door opens; at 9:05 Elia leaves; at 9:12 Nera calls. Where’s Iona in that sequence?
The medical window starts after the only record consistent with Iona leaving.
pushback: No, the 9:12 call proves Nera was alive. It doesn’t place Iona beside her.
Which timestamp actually closes the rear-door possibility?
concede: I’ll accept that the coat plan looks bad. It still doesn’t answer the location question.
final: The times establish a homicide, but they don’t complete the identification.

jurors.label: Juror 5 — Dev
jurors.persona: Dev begins on the prosecution side but changes course when independent records do not support the same inference.

agree: The records are independent, but they don’t converge on Iona staying.
The rear audit and the fracture limit point away from the prosecution’s completed timeline.
pushback: I started with guilt because the coat request looked planned. What independent item takes the next step?
Are we combining gaps, or combining proof?
concede: I’ve changed my view. The clasp and transit evidence corroborate details, not the alleged killing.
final: Separate records matter only if they prove the proposition we’re deciding.

jurors.label: Juror 6 — Esra
jurors.persona: Esra asks experts to translate ranges and limits before giving scientific language extra weight.

agree: ‘Recent’ sounded precise until Dr Sann said it meant a whole day.
The match tells us whose bracelet it came from. It doesn’t tell us when it broke.
pushback: Can someone point to a test that separates four o’clock from nine fifteen?
I’m not ignoring the clasp. I’m refusing to give it a timestamp it doesn’t have.
concede: All right, I’d been treating possession at death as contact at death. They aren’t the same.
final: The science supports a match, not the prosecution’s time of contact.

jurors.label: Juror 7 — Fia
jurors.persona: Fia distrusts bargains and sometimes catches herself demanding answers from the accused.

agree: Elia told the truth about travelling only after immunity. Why should I trust the part no record confirms?
Yes, the bargain doesn’t erase her evidence; it means we test every piece.
pushback: Hold on. Iona arranged the coat trick, and I want an honest reason why.
Elia’s account isn’t clean just because one travel record matches it.
concede: The transit card confirms Elia left. I agree it stops there.
burden_drift: I was about to say Iona should prove the rear-door user. That’s backwards, isn’t it?
final: Once I put the burden back, Elia’s assumption couldn’t carry the missing step.

jurors.label: Juror 8 — Garen
jurors.persona: Garen sees the coat request as planning, yet keeps asking what that planning was intended to achieve.

agree: The request was deliberate, but was it a plan to avoid Nera or a plan to kill her?
Planning a false appearance is probative. It still needs a connection to the homicide.
pushback: I’m not comfortable dismissing a carefully arranged deception as childish.
If the coat wasn’t about the killing, what was it about?
concede: I accept the rear-door timing gives the lesser explanation real support.
final: The prosecution proved a deception, but not the murderous purpose it alleged.

jurors.label: Juror 9 — Hale
jurors.persona: Hale speaks tentatively, revisits first impressions, and distinguishes an understandable lie from a reliable account.

agree: Maybe Elia was frightened. But that explains the lie; it doesn’t verify the accusation, does it?
I think the rear-door record matters because it supports something other than Elia’s assumption.
pushback: I’m still bothered that Iona asked Elia to hide her face.
Could the clasp in Nera’s hand really be only coincidence? I’m not sure.
concede: Yes—I was letting the strange coat request answer a different question.
final: I can believe parts of Elia’s account without being sure Iona killed Nera.

jurors.label: Juror 10 — Iri
jurors.persona: Iri keeps the discussion orderly by asking the room to test one element and one inference at a time.

agree: Let’s mark what is agreed: Nera was murdered after 9:12. Identity remains separate.
The rear-door record does not establish an alibi, but it prevents us from assuming continued presence.
pushback: Which element are we addressing with that point?
We can consider the strands together only after stating what each strand proves.
concede: I accept the prosecution’s evidence establishes a deliberate killing. It still has to establish Iona caused it.
burden_correct: Fia, you caught it: Iona doesn’t have to identify the rear-door user. The prosecution has to exclude the reasonable possibility.
final: I’m not sure the identity element was proved, so the legal direction determines my verdict.

jurors.label: Juror 11 — Joss
jurors.persona: Joss notices changed accounts quickly, but will revise a sharp first reaction when the actual words are read back.

agree: Read Iona’s first words again. She denied a struggle, not every bit of contact.
The lab can’t time the break. That knocks out the point I thought was strongest.
pushback: She left out the rear door. I’m allowed to think that looks bad.
Why should we accept Iona’s correction when we reject Elia’s?
concede: All right, I overstated the first interview. The omission hurts credibility; it isn’t a contradiction on the clasp.
final: The changed account raised suspicion, but the expert couldn’t give it a time link.

jurors.label: Juror 12 — Kemi
